sources.title: Large Language Models Are Unreliable for Cyber Threat Intelligence
key_claims: LLMs cannot guarantee sufficient performance on real-size (350-report) CTI evaluation while also being inconsistent across repeated queries and overconfident in stated certainty.

Few-shot learning and fine-tuning only partially improve results, indicating the unreliability persists across zero-shot, few-shot, and fine-tuning paradigms rather than being solved by more examples.
Reliability for CTI should be measured as a multi-dimensional property (accuracy + consistency + confidence calibration), not accuracy alone.

The 3 tested LLMs were gpt4o (OpenAI), gemini-1.5-pro-latest (Google), and mistral-large-2 (Mistral); consistency was measured via bootstrapped confidence intervals across 10 re-prompts per input, staying narrow for information-extraction tasks (max CI width 0.02, e.g. Gemini campaign-retrieval precision/recall CI [0.73, 0.74]) but widening notably for information-generation tasks (max CI width 0.06, e.g. Gemini CVE-generation recall CI [0.19, 0.25], a ~27% relative range).

Confidence calibration (ECE and Brier score, reported for gpt4o) was markedly worse for information-generation than information-extraction sub-tasks, e.g. CVE-generation ECE 0.15 (zero-shot), and calibration did not uniformly improve with fine-tuning: Campaign-extraction ECE rose from 0.25 (zero-shot) to 0.48 (fine-tuned) and CVE-generation ECE rose from 0.15 to 0.91, though CVE-extraction ECE improved from 0.28 to 0.18 -- effects were inconsistent across sub-tasks rather than uniform partial improvement.

Fine-tuning and few-shot prompting frequently degraded raw extraction accuracy rather than improving it: GPT-4o APT-entity extraction precision/recall fell from 0.87 (zero-shot) to 0.68 (fine-tuned), a ~22% relative drop, and few-shot prompting reduced APT extraction performance by ~8% for Gemini/Mistral -- sharpening the abstract's 'only partially improve' framing into a more specific finding that additional training examples or fine-tuning can actively worsen both accuracy and calibration on certain CTI sub-tasks.

sources.title: CTIBench: A Benchmark for Evaluating LLMs in Cyber Threat Intelligence
key_claims: Task difficulty is highly uneven across CTI sub-tasks: best-model accuracy reaches 71-72% on knowledge recall (CTI-MCQ) and CVE-to-CWE mapping (CTI-RCM), but MITRE ATT&CK technique extraction (CTI-ATE) F1 tops out at 0.64 even for the strongest model (GPT-4-turbo).

On threat-actor attribution (CTI-TAA over 50 real reports), every tested model's 'plausible-sounding' attribution rate is far higher than its 'correct' attribution rate (e.g. GPT-4-turbo: 86% plausible vs 52% correct), a quantified instance of confident-but-wrong CTI output.
No evaluated model (GPT-4-turbo, GPT-3.5-turbo, Gemini-1.5, LLAMA3-70B, LLAMA3-8B) exceeded ~72% on any single task, showing scale alone had not solved CTI reliability as of this 2024-era benchmark.

sources.title: Revealing the True Indicators: Understanding and Improving IoC Extraction From Threat Reports
key_claims: The authors built PRISM, described as the first open, fully manually-validated benchmark of 1,791 IoCs from 50 real-world threat reports, to ground-truth IoC extraction evaluation.
Their hybrid regex+LLM+human-validation system LANCE reached 97.6% overall F1 against PRISM, outperforming IoC Searcher+whitelist (76%), AlienVault OTX (72%), and VirusTotal threshold=1 (86%).

Human-in-the-loop use of LANCE reduced junior analysts' manual annotation time by 43% and models trained on LANCE-labeled data outperformed VirusTotal-labeled training data by over 6% F1, suggesting narrow, human-validated LLM assistance is far more reliable for mechanical IoC extraction than for open-ended CTI reasoning tasks (contrast with src-0001, src-0002).

sources.title: EU cyber agency secretly uses AI for reports – and gets caught
key_claims: Two ENISA 'Threat Landscape 2025' reports (published Oct/Nov 2025) contained AI-hallucinated citations; one report had 26 of 492 footnotes incorrect, discovered by Westfälische Hochschule researchers after finding non-functional source links.

A specific hallucination fingerprint was identified: a passage attributed the name 'APT29' to Microsoft's own naming convention, when Microsoft actually calls that group 'Midnight Blizzard' — a technical signature consistent with LLM-generated text.

ENISA's official response called the errors 'human errors' while confirming AI was permitted for 'minor editorial revisions', illustrating institutional under-acknowledgment of AI-attributable failure even after public exposure.

sources.title: CyberSOCEval: Benchmarking LLMs Capabilities for Malware Analysis and Threat Intelligence Reasoning
key_claims: Released by CrowdStrike/Meta-affiliated authors as part of CyberSecEval 4; larger/more modern LLMs perform better on malware analysis and threat-intel reasoning tasks, consistent with scaling laws, as of 2025-era models.

Reasoning models using test-time scaling do not get the same performance boost on these CTI/malware tasks that they get on coding and math benchmarks, suggesting generic reasoning post-training does not transfer well to cybersecurity threat analysis.
As of publication, 'current LLMs are far from saturating' the CyberSOCEval evaluations — substantial measured unreliability/headroom remains industry-wide, not just in academic benchmarks.

sources.title: Uncovering Vulnerabilities of LLM-Assisted Cyber Threat Intelligence
key_claims: LLM failures in CTI stem from properties of the threat landscape itself (heterogeneous, volatile, fragmented evidence) more than from generic model architecture issues, per a human-in-the-loop failure-categorization framework applied across the CTI lifecycle.

The paper's three identified failure patterns (spurious correlations, contradictory knowledge, constrained generalization) occur across all four CTI pipeline stages it defines (Contextualization, Attribution, Prediction, Mitigation), not concentrated in reasoning-heavy stages -- evidence that a simple mechanical-extraction-vs-open-ended-reasoning binary may be too coarse to explain where reliability breaks down.

Within one consistent study/methodology, reliability varies enormously by specific sub-task (F1/AUC roughly 0.20-0.90 across tasks and models, e.g. Source Reliability Scoring AUC 0.912 vs 0.547 for different models on the same task), directly demonstrating task-dependent reliability in a single unified design rather than only via cross-benchmark synthesis; targeted causal-intervention mitigations produced measurable but comparatively modest gains on attribution-adjacent tasks (e.g. +0.055 accuracy on Threat Actor Linking) relative to LANCE's mechanical-IoC-extraction gain (src-0003).

sources.title: CyberThreat-Eval: Can Large Language Models Automate Real-World Threat Research?
key_claims: On an expert-annotated benchmark drawn from a real company's daily CTI workflow (1310 IoCs), vanilla LLMs extracting IoCs reached precision 0.8240 (GPT-4o) and 0.8503 (o3-mini); fine-tuning raised GPT-4o to 0.8846 but fine-tuned GPT-4o-mini fell to 0.6944. Recall and F1 are not reported for this task and the paper gives no reason for their absence.

In the same study and table, MITRE ATT&CK TTP identification scored far lower than IoC extraction -- precision 0.2787 / recall 0.2270 (GPT-4o), 0.3480 / 0.1759 (o3-mini) -- a second within-study demonstration that mechanical indicator extraction and technique mapping are very different in difficulty for the same models on the same corpus.

Automated triage showed an extreme precision/recall asymmetry (recall Accepted 0.90-1.00 but precision Accepted 0.27-0.40 across all four models): the models accept nearly everything a human analyst would reject.

Authors are affiliated with Microsoft Research, Microsoft and HKUST, are unaffiliated with PRISM/LANCE's authors, and the paper does not cite arXiv 2506.11325 (src-0003) -- making this an independent measurement rather than a replication attempt or a critique.

sources.title: Benchmarking Large Language Models for IoC Recovery under Adversarial Code Obfuscation and Encryption
key_claims: Recovering an IoC that appears in plain text is near-free for current LLMs: ~100% detection at baseline and through four levels of syntactic obfuscation (variable renaming, Base64) for GPT-4 Turbo, Claude 3 Sonnet, Gemini 1.5 Pro and Grok-2, over a 336-program JavaScript dataset.

Cryptographic concealment (XOR, AES-256) collapses detection to roughly 0-1% and the failure persists through combined transformations, identifying encryption as an adversary-controlled evasion of LLM-based indicator recovery.

SCOPE LIMIT, do not cite as a replication of src-0003: the task is recovering a planted indicator from JavaScript source code under adversarial transformation, not separating malicious from benign indicators in narrative threat reports; the per-level percentages were read from the results tables by automated fetch and are approximate pending a verbatim table pull.
